blocks.text: What Damir says of the rachama also fits the vulture, namely that it lays either a single egg or at most two. For Aristotle says of the vulture in History, book 6, chapter 5, Τίκτουσι δὲ δύο ὠὰ οἱ γῦπες [Tiktousi de dyo ōa hoi gypes], Vultures lay two eggs. And in book 9, chapter 11, Τίκτει δ᾽ ἓν ὠὸν, ἢ δύο τὰ πλεῖστα· [Tiktei d' hen ōon, ē dyo ta pleista] It lays one egg, or at most two. Pliny, in the place cited above: Their young are indeed often seen, usually in pairs.

It is also characteristic of the vulture, as we read of the rachama in the Bellunensis, that it eats putrid flesh; and in Alkazuinius, تطير خلف العساكر لتاكل من [taṭīru khalfa al-ʿasākir li-taʾkula min] [III, 62] جيف [jiyaf] It flies behind armies in order to feed on corpses. Hence in Homer, throughout, those who have been slain
the vultures devour. And the same men are said to be
— — γύπεσσιν πολὺ φίλτεροι, ἢ ἀλόχοισιν [gypessin poly philteroi, ē alochoisin],

far dearer to the vultures than to their wives. Indeed, on the testimony of Herodorus of Pontus in Plutarch, Roman Questions, Question 93, the vulture οὐδενὸς ἅπτεται ζῶντος, χρῆται δὲ τοῖς ἄλλοις ἀποθανοῦσιν [oudenos haptetai zōntos, chrētai de tois allois apothanousin], touches nothing living, but feeds only on the dead. Hence Lucretius, book 4, line 680:
Though bees are drawn from far by the scent of honey, And vultures by corpses. — —
Or as the greedy vulture looks about for some body That it can see lying beneath no earth.
Here are the dread birds, and the vulture fed on corpses.
Gregory of Nazianzus, Poem 163, On the Adornment of Women:
— — νεκροῖς ἀμφιέπουσι γῦπες [nekrois amphiepousi gypes], — — the vulture, of course, loves a corpse.
And the bite of vultures, far more effective [col. 309] At devouring morsels of dead flesh.

Plutarch, On Natural Causes, Question 26: Τὰ κενέβρια τὸν γῦπα κινεῖ, καὶ προσάγεται πόῤῥωθεν· [Ta kenebria ton gypa kinei, kai prosagetai porrhōthen] Carrion flesh stirs the vulture and draws it from afar. And in the book On Profiting from One's Enemies: Καθάπερ οἱ γῦπες ἐπὶ τὰς ὀσμὰς τῶν διεφθορότων σωμάτων φέρονται· [Kathaper hoi gypes epi tas osmas tōn diephthorotōn sōmatōn pherontai] As vultures are borne towards the smell of corpses. Aelian, History, book 2, chapter 46: Γὺψ νεκρῷ πολέμιος, ἐσθίει γοῦν ἐμπεσὼν, ὡς ἐχθρόν· [Gyps nekrō polemios, esthiei goun empesōn, hōs echthron] The vulture is hostile to the dead, and falling upon it devours it as if it were an enemy. It is moreover believed to foresee those who will soon die. Aelian in the same place: Φυλάσσει τεθνηξόμενον. καὶ μέν τοι καὶ ταῖς ἐκδήμοις στρατιαῖς ἕπονται γῦπες, καὶ μάλα μαντικῶς, ὅτι γε εἰς πόλεμον χωροῦσιν εἰδότες, καὶ ὅτι μάχη πᾶσα ἐργάζεται νεκροὺς, καὶ τοῦτο ἐγνωκότες· [Phylassei tethnēxomenon. kai men toi kai tais ekdēmois stratiais hepontai gypes, kai mala mantikōs, hoti ge eis polemon chōrousin eidotes, kai hoti machē pasa ergazetai nekrous, kai touto egnōkotes] It watches one who is about to die. Vultures also follow armies marching abroad, by a kind of foreknowledge, since they know that they are setting out for war, and know this too, that every battle produces some slaughter. Philes, On Animals, chapter 2: [III, 63] Πλὴν μαντικὴν ἔχουσιν οἱ γῦπες φύσιν· Καὶ γὰρ συνεκδημοῦσι τοῖς μαχουμένοις, Τῶν σωμάτων ἐλπίδι πεσουμένων τότε. [Plēn mantikēn echousin hoi gypes physin; kai gar synekdēmousi tois machoumenois, tōn sōmatōn elpidi pesoumenōn tote.]

Moreover, vultures have a prophetic nature: for they travel abroad with those who are about to fight, in hope of the corpses that will then fall. In Pliny, Umbricius, the most skilled of the haruspices, reports that they fly three or two days beforehand to where there will be corpses. Hence Plautus in the Truculentus, in the scene Piscis:
— — see how now, like vultures, they foretell three days beforehand on what day they will eat.
